disclosed_facts.fact: Amazon reports Amazon Web Services (AWS) as one of three reportable segments, serving developers and enterprises of all sizes through AWS, which offers a broad set of on-demand technology services including compute, storage, database, analytics, and artificial intelligence and machine learning services — i.e., the company itself sells the compute.

Competition disclosure identifies competitors that provide information technology services or products, including on-premises or cloud-based infrastructure and tools and services relating to artificial intelligence, positioning AWS's cloud infrastructure business against other AI-infrastructure providers.

Purchases of property and equipment of $54,208 million in Q2 2026 and $98,411 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026 (vs. $32,183 million and $57,202 million in the prior-year periods); trailing twelve months $173,028 million — a large step-up in capital spend on infrastructure.

Property and equipment, net grew from $357,025 million at December 31, 2025 to $446,046 million at June 30, 2026; operating lease assets grew from $86,054 million to $92,743 million, with long-term lease liabilities of $94,338 million — an owned-plus-leased infrastructure base, not broken out between data centers and fulfillment/logistics.

Long-term debt rose from $65,648 million at December 31, 2025 to $128,894 million at June 30, 2026, with $66,998 million of proceeds from long-term debt in the six months ended June 30, 2026, funding the elevated investing outflows.
Total net sales of $200,606 million in Q2 2026, of which net service sales were $123,004 million; the supplied text does not disaggregate AWS segment revenue or any AI-compute revenue.
Technology and infrastructure operating expense of $33,158 million in Q2 2026 and $62,725 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026 (up from $27,166 million and $50,160 million).

Human capital disclosure cites intense competition for technical staff including for artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies; AWS is led by a CEO (Matthew S. Garman) whose prior roles include VP, AWS Compute Services and VP, EC2.

On June 8, 2026, the Company entered into a material definitive agreement creating a direct financial obligation (Item 1.01 / Item 2.03); the supplied excerpt does not identify the counterparty, amount, or subject matter.
Closed sale of $750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of notes on July 9, 2026, and C$1,250,000,000 of 3.400% notes on June 12, 2026; use of proceeds not disclosed in the supplied excerpts.

primary_business: Online/physical stores, third-party seller services, advertising, and AWS cloud infrastructure — organized as North America, International, and AWS segments
key_unknowns: AWS segment revenue, growth and operating income are not present in the supplied text (10-K excerpt stops before Item 7/Note 10 segment information; 10-Q excerpt does not include the segment note).
No disclosed AI-compute revenue, AI backlog/remaining performance obligations, or any $/% of revenue attributable to AI workloads.
No named AI-compute customer contracts, take-or-pay commitments, capacity reservations, or quantified TCV in the supplied excerpts.
Capital expenditures are not broken out between AWS data-center/AI infrastructure and fulfillment/logistics/other; no disclosed contracted MW, land, substation or grid-interconnect positions.
No disclosure in the supplied text about custom silicon (e.g., in-house AI chips), power procurement, colocation/leasing mix, or third-party data-center leases.
Subject matter, counterparty and terms of the June 8, 2026 material definitive agreement are not in the supplied excerpt.
Purpose/use of proceeds for the 2026 debt issuances is not stated in the supplied excerpts.
No quantification of 'data gravity' assets (e.g., stored data volumes, egress/interconnection economics) for AWS.

disclosed_facts.fact: Microsoft describes itself as offering cloud-based solutions providing customers with AI, software, services, platforms and content, and states its AI offerings span every layer of the technology stack — including the intelligent cloud platform ambition to provide the foundation for customers' digital workloads.

The 10-K states the Microsoft Cloud business benefits from three economies of scale grounded in its own datacenters: datacenters deploying computational resources at significantly lower cost per unit than smaller ones; datacenters that aggregate diverse customer, geographic and application demand to improve utilization of computing, storage and network resources; and multi-tenancy locations lowering application maintenance labor costs — i.e., operating its own scaled compute footprint.

Intelligent Cloud is one of three reportable segments used to report financial performance, per Item 1 segment description (segment revenue detail referenced to Note 18, not shown in the supplied text).

Additions to property and equipment of $30,876 million in the quarter ended March 31, 2026 and $80,146 million for the nine months ended March 31, 2026, versus $16,745 million and $47,472 million in the prior-year periods.

Property and equipment, net grew to $283,228 million at March 31, 2026 from $204,966 million at June 30, 2025, with accumulated depreciation of $111,723 million; operating lease right-of-use assets of $24,403 million.

Total revenue of $82,886 million for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 (up from $70,066 million) and $241,832 million for the nine months, with 'Service and other' revenue of $67,797 million in the quarter — blended, not broken out to cloud/AI compute.

Stated strategy of 'building and running cloud-based services in ways that utilize ubiquitous computing' and 'leading the AI platform wave across our solution areas,' plus providing 'trusted platforms' for frontier AI transformation.

Stated intent to provide 'a unified intelligence layer for enterprise AI to ground AI in a continuously evolving understanding of an organization's data' — a data-gravity ambition on Microsoft's own platform, described as strategy without disclosed economics.

Productivity and Business Processes segment products (Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Microsoft 365 Copilot, LinkedIn, Dynamics 365) are described as AI-powered application/SaaS offerings, i.e., layers above the compute platform.

More Personal Computing-related activity described in Item 1 includes designing and selling devices (PCs, tablets, gaming consoles, accessories) and delivering online advertising — activity distinct from selling compute or owning interconnection.

primary_business: A technology company selling cloud computing, AI, software and productivity platforms plus devices, reported in three segments (Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, More Personal Computing).
key_unknowns: The supplied 10-K text is truncated at the Competition discussion; Azure/Intelligent Cloud revenue, Microsoft Cloud revenue, commercial bookings and remaining performance obligation figures (Note 18 segment data, MD&A) are not present in the stream.
No AI-compute revenue is broken out — no $ or % of revenue attributed to Azure AI services, AI infrastructure, or compute sold to AI model developers.
No disclosed contracted capacity metrics: no MW, no datacenter square footage, no substation/grid interconnect ownership, no cross-connect or interconnection detail.
No named counterparty compute agreements (e.g., model-developer capacity commitments) with binding terms, TCV, take-or-pay or prepayment appear anywhere in the supplied text.

The $80.1B nine-month capex and $283B PP&E are not disaggregated between AI/datacenter infrastructure and other uses, nor between owned facilities and finance/operating leases (leased vs. owned interconnection therefore unresolved).
Equity and other investments rose from $15,405M to $33,683M with no disclosed composition in the supplied text (any AI-related investment or related-party compute arrangement is not described).
Purchase commitments, unconditional purchase obligations and lease commitments notes are not included in the supplied 10-Q excerpt.
'Data gravity' is not quantified — no disclosed measure of data stored, workload stickiness, or associated revenue.
8-Ks in the stream are earnings-furnishing and governance items only; the referenced press-release exhibits (Exhibit 99.1) with segment/Azure commentary are not included in the supplied text.

disclosed_facts.fact: Alphabet reports Google in two segments, Google Services and Google Cloud; Google Cloud is described as helping customers build for the future, improve productivity, reduce costs and unlock new growth engines — i.e., Alphabet operates a scaled hyperscaler cloud business as a reported segment.

The filing describes AI-optimized infrastructure as the foundation of its 'full-stack approach' and a key differentiator, powering its own products (Search, YouTube) and supporting the services provided to Google Cloud customers.

Technical infrastructure allows Alphabet to use and offer customers a range of AI accelerator options, including specialized GPUs and its own custom-built TPUs, such as Ironwood, its seventh-generation TPU — i.e., selling AI compute options to cloud customers.
Stated focus on driving efficiencies in its data centers to leverage its technical infrastructure to deliver products and services at increasing scale while enabling research and model development.
Own data-gravity/distribution scale disclosed: trillions of searches on Google every year; all 15 half-billion-user products, including seven with two billion users, use Gemini models.
Google Cloud offerings for customers include Gemini Enterprise and Gemini for Google Workspace (enterprise-facing platform services delivered on its own infrastructure).

Balance sheet shows property and equipment, net rising from $246,597 million at December 31, 2025 to $321,212 million at June 30, 2026 (a ~$74.6 billion increase in six months), consistent with disclosed large-scale infrastructure investment; the filing text supplied does not attribute this to AI compute specifically.

Consolidated revenues of $119,796 million for Q2 2026 and $229,692 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, reported on a blended consolidated basis in the supplied text with no Google Cloud or AI-compute revenue line broken out.

Statement that AI is a profound platform shift and that the company aims to build the most advanced, safe and responsible AI, having invested more than $200 billion in research and development over the last five years (R&D total, not attributed to compute infrastructure).
Frontier model development (Gemini 3) and centralized AI research are reported in Alphabet-level activities — this is the model layer, not the compute/interconnection layer.

Google Services revenue is generated primarily from advertising on Google Search & other properties, YouTube and Google Network properties, plus consumer subscriptions, Play platforms and Pixel devices — advertising/consumer economics, distinct from selling compute.

primary_business: A collection of businesses led by Google — reported as Google Services (ads, Android, Play, Search, YouTube, devices) and Google Cloud, plus Other Bets — with AI-optimized technical infrastructure underpinning both.
key_unknowns: Google Cloud segment revenue, growth and margin are not present in the supplied text; no AI-compute or TPU/GPU revenue is broken out.
No disclosed contracted cloud/AI compute capacity: no MW, no committed capacity figures, no backlog/remaining performance obligation amounts in the supplied excerpts.
No named cloud customers or executed compute agreements with binding terms (minimum volume, take-or-pay, TCV, prepayment) appear in the stream.
Capital expenditure guidance/amounts for data centers are not in the supplied text; the ~$74.6bn increase in net property and equipment is not attributed to AI compute or broken out by asset type.

Data center ownership vs. lease mix, land, substation and grid interconnect ownership, and any power procurement arrangements are not disclosed in the supplied excerpts (Item 2 Properties text not included).
No disclosure in the stream on cross-connect/interconnection assets, network peering economics, or third-party colocation reliance.
Whether TPU/Ironwood capacity is sold externally beyond Google Cloud, and on what commercial terms, is not disclosed.
The 8-Ks in the stream contain only cover-page/securities registration data with no described transaction relating to compute infrastructure.
